title: CNA After the Exam: Registry Listing and the 24-Month Rule
description: How a passed CNA exam turns into a nurse aide registry entry, what a nursing home must check before you start, and how to avoid losing your listing.
intro: In most jobs, a certificate is a piece of paper you keep. For a nurse aide it works differently. What a nursing home looks at is your entry on the state nurse aide registry, and that entry can be removed if you stop working. The basic rules come from federal regulations for nursing homes that take part in Medicare or Medicaid (Title 42 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 483). Each state runs its own registry and can add its own steps, but it cannot go below these rules. This guide explains what happens between passing the test and your first shift, and what keeps your listing active over the years.

sections.heading: From a passing score to a registry entry
sections.body:
To pass the competency evaluation, you must pass **both** parts: the written (or oral) test and the skills demonstration. Passing one part alone does not put you on the registry.

Once the state finds you competent, federal rules (42 CFR 483.154) say the record of your success must be added to the registry **within 30 days**. So it is normal to wait a little before your name shows up in an online lookup.

If you do not pass, you must be told which areas you missed, and you must get **at least three chances** to take the evaluation. A state may set a maximum number of tries, but that number cannot be lower than three.

sections.heading: What the registry shows about you
sections.body:
Under 42 CFR 483.156, the registry must hold at least:

- your full name and the information needed to identify you
- the date you became eligible for the registry by passing the program
- any finding by the state survey agency of **abuse, neglect, or misappropriation of property** (taking a resident's money or belongings)

The date of eligibility and any such findings must be given to anyone who asks. A finding is added within 10 working days and stays **permanently**, unless it was made in error, a court found you not guilty, or the state is told of your death. If there is a finding, you may add your own statement disputing it, and any registry answer that reports the finding must include your statement.

Two more points help you: the state may not charge you any fee related to registration, and you have the right to see your own record and get mistakes corrected.

sections.heading: What a nursing home must check before your first shift
sections.body:
42 CFR 483.35(d) sets hiring rules that every nursing home in these programs must follow:

1. **Registry check.** Before you work as a nurse aide, the facility must get registry confirmation that you met the competency requirements.
2. **Other states.** The facility must also ask every other state registry it believes may have information on you. If you trained or worked in another state, tell the employer.
3. **Just passed, not listed yet.** If you can prove you recently passed a state-approved program but are not on the registry yet, the facility may let you start, but it must follow up to make sure you actually get listed.
4. **The 4-month limit.** A facility cannot use someone as a full-time nurse aide for more than 4 months unless that person is competent and has completed a state-approved program.

The same rules apply to temporary, per diem, and leased (agency) staff, not only permanent employees.

sections.heading: The 24-month rule: how a listing lapses
sections.body:
This is the rule that surprises people who take a break from care work. Federal rules connect two things to a gap of **24 consecutive months**:

- **The registry** must remove the entry of anyone who has performed no nursing or nursing-related services for 24 consecutive months (42 CFR 483.156).
- **The nursing home** must require a **new** training and competency evaluation program, or a new competency evaluation program, if since your last program there has been a continuous 24-month period in which you did not provide nursing or nursing-related services **for pay** (42 CFR 483.35(d)(6)).

The wording is about one unbroken gap, counted from your most recent program, not about total hours. An entry with a documented finding of abuse, neglect, or misappropriation is not removed for lack of work.

States set the details of how they confirm your work, such as forms or renewal steps. Your state registry is the place to ask what proof it accepts.

sections.heading: Yearly requirements once you are working
sections.body:
Being hired is not the last check. The facility must give every nurse aide a **performance review at least once every 12 months** and plan in-service education based on what that review finds (42 CFR 483.35(d)(7)).

That in-service training must be at least **12 hours a year** and must include dementia management and resident abuse prevention (42 CFR 483.95(g)). It also has to cover weak areas found in your review, and if you care for residents with cognitive impairment, it must address their care too. Keeping your own copies of these training records is a simple way to show your history later.

sections.heading: Who pays for your training
sections.body:
42 CFR 483.152 has a rule many new aides do not know. If you already work for a nursing home, or have a job offer from one, on the day you start a nurse aide training program, you **cannot be charged** for any part of it, including textbooks and required materials.

If you paid for training on your own and then get hired, or get a job offer, by a nursing home within **12 months** of finishing, the state must provide for paying back your costs on a pro rata basis (a share for the time you work as a nurse aide). Ask your state registry or employer how that is handled where you live.

sections.heading: A short plan for this month
sections.body:
1. A few weeks after your results, look yourself up on your state registry and check that your name and eligibility date are right.
2. Write down the date you start your first paid nurse aide job. Keep pay stubs or employer letters in one folder.
3. If you plan a long break, put a reminder well before the 24-month mark and ask your registry what counts as work.
4. Still studying? On this site, the Role of the Nurse Aide area makes up 16 of the 60 scored items in the NNAAP outline, and its legal and ethical chapter here is where registry and abuse reporting questions sit.

faq.question: Does my CNA listing move with me to another state?
faq.answer: Each state keeps its own registry, so a new state decides how to add you, and the steps differ. Federal rules only require a nursing home to check every state registry it believes may have information on you. Contact the registry in the state where you plan to work before you move.

faq.question: Can I start working before my name appears on the registry?
faq.answer: At a nursing home, possibly. If you can prove you recently passed a state-approved program and are not listed yet, the facility may let you work, but it must follow up to make sure you are actually registered.

faq.question: Do these rules apply to hospitals and home care?
faq.answer: The rules in this guide are written for nursing homes in Medicare and Medicaid. Other employers, such as hospitals and home health agencies, follow their own rules and state laws, so ask the employer what it requires.
